**On the Pleasure of Unfinished Things**

There is a particular pleasure in a notebook with twelve pages left, a saved draft no one will read, a route home that takes longer than necessary. We spend so much time finishing—closing tabs, checking boxes, turning intentions into announcements—that we forget the quiet usefulness of the unfinished.

An unfinished thing is not a failure. It is a room with the door left open. It lets in air.

I like to think of the mind as a city at dusk: some windows lit, some dark, a few streets half-repaired, a bakery still awake, a bus arriving late but arriving. Nothing is entirely resolved. That is what makes it a city and not a diagram.

There is a kind of attention that only arrives when you stop trying to extract a lesson from everything. A walk without a podcast. A cup of tea going cold because you are looking out the window. A conversation that wanders past its point and finds something better. These are not wasted minutes. They are the margins where the actual text of a life gets written.

We are taught to admire sharpness: the clean argument, the polished sentence, the decisive plan. But softness has its own intelligence. So does hesitation. So does the second look at a thing you thought you already understood.

Maybe the most useful question is not “What does this mean?” but “What is this like when I stop rushing it?”

A tree in winter looks dead until you remember it is not waiting to be rescued. It is doing something slow and invisible. The roots are not on holiday. The buds are already there, tiny and stubborn, under the bark. There is no emergency. There is only the long work of becoming.

I want to keep some of that in mind. Not every silence needs to be filled. Not every idea needs to become a project. Not every feeling needs to be solved before dinner. Some things are better carried than concluded.

So here is to the half-read book on the arm of the chair, the playlist that never got named, the letter begun and set aside because the right word had not arrived yet. Here is to the walk that takes the long way. The map with a blank space in the middle. The plan that has room in it for weather.

Nothing has to be finished to be real. Some of the truest things are still in progress—quietly, stubbornly, like roots in winter.
